what_its_for: Letermovir is an antiviral medicine used to prevent a viral infection called cytomegalovirus (CMV) from coming back or getting worse in adults and children who have received a bone marrow or stem cell transplant. CMV is a common virus that can cause serious illness in people with weakened immune systems.
how_to_take: Take letermovir by mouth once a day, with or without food. Swallow the tablet whole — do not crush, chew, or split it. Try to take it at the same time every day to help you remember. If you are in the hospital, this medicine may also be given to you through an IV (into your vein) by a healthcare provider.
dosing: The usual adult dose is 480 mg once daily by mouth. However, if you are also taking a medicine called cyclosporine, your dose will be lowered to 240 mg once daily. Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your weight and other medicines you take. Always follow your doctor's specific dosing instructions and never change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember on the same day. If you do not remember until the next day, skip the missed dose and take your next regular dose at the usual time. Do not take two doses in one day to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store letermovir tablets at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep the tablets in their original container with the cap tightly closed. Protect from moisture and light. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush medicines down the toilet or pour them down a drain unless instructed to do so. Ask your pharmacist about the best way to dispose of unused medicine.
what_to_avoid: Avoid missing doses, as this can allow the CMV virus to grow and become harder to treat. Tell your doctor about ALL medicines, vitamins, and herbal supplements you take, because letermovir can interact with many other medications. Avoid taking medicines that contain pimozide or ergot alkaloids (such as ergotamine) while on letermovir without talking to your doctor first. Avoid drinking large amounts of grapefruit juice, as it may affect how this medicine works in your body.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you experience any of the following: nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea that is severe or does not go away; unusual tiredness or weakness; yellowing of your skin or eyes (jaundice); stomach pain; fast or irregular heartbeat; signs of liver problems such as dark urine or pale stools; any new or worsening symptoms; or signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, hives, swelling of the face or throat, or difficulty breathing. Also call your doctor if you feel your condition is not improving or if you have any questions about your treatment.
when_it_works: Letermovir starts working right away to help prevent CMV infection, but you may not feel any different because it is working to prevent a problem rather than treat symptoms you already have. It is very important to keep taking it every day for as long as your doctor prescribes — usually for about 100 days after your transplant. Do not stop taking it early without talking to your doctor, even if you feel well.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. It is not known if letermovir is safe during pregnancy or if it passes into breast milk. Your doctor will help you weigh the risks and benefits. Children: Letermovir can be used in children who have had a stem cell transplant, but the dose is based on the child's weight. Your child's doctor will determine the correct dose. Kidney or liver problems: Your doctor may need to adjust your dose or monitor you more closely if you have kidney or liver disease. Always tell your doctor and pharmacist about all your health conditions before starting this medicine.
